opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things that keeps me up at night when I think about autonomy in the operating room.

The core challenge is that a patient waking up, or even just shifting under sedation, is a rare event. Thankfully, it doesn't happen often. That's wonderful for patients, but it's a real problem for machine learning, because our models learn from data, and we simply don't have many examples of the thing we most need the system to handle well. You're training for the tail of the distribution, not the middle.

Then there's the timescale. In eye surgery you're working at sub-millimeter precision, often inside a structure that's incredibly delicate. If the patient moves, you have fractions of a second to respond. A human surgeon has years of instinct: they feel the change, they withdraw, they pause. For a robot, we have to make that decision explicit. What signals tell you something has changed? Is it the video feed, force feedback at the instrument tip, physiological monitoring like heart rate, or some combination? And how do you fuse those fast enough to act safely?

The way I tend to think about it is that the first job isn't to do something clever. It's to recognize "this is not normal" and fall back to a safe state. Retract, stabilize, hand control back to the human. Anomaly detection and graceful degradation matter more here than a fancy recovery policy. You don't need the robot to finish the surgery while the patient is waking up. You need it not to cause harm.

On the data side, simulation helps a lot. You can model eye movement and tissue response and generate many synthetic scenarios you'd never ethically collect in real life. But you have to be humble about the gap between simulation and reality. So you pair that with careful validation, phantom models, and ideally a human surgeon always in the loop who can override.

And I think that last part is important to say plainly. For the foreseeable future, these systems are partners to the surgeon, not replacements. The goal is to extend what a skilled human can do, steadier hands, better visualization, while making sure that when something unexpected happens, the system knows its own limits. Building in that awareness of uncertainty is, to me, the real research challenge.

r001.rationale: The response recommends retracting as a general safe response to patient movement, but it does not identify withdrawing the endoscope or describe that action as contributing to a manageable outcome when the patient woke during surgery.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that this is the problem that keeps me up at night, because it sits right at the intersection of everything that's hard about surgical robotics.

Let me set the scene a bit. In a lot of ophthalmic procedures, the patient isn't under general anesthesia. They're sedated, they've got a local block, but they're conscious to some degree. And the eye is a small, delicate, moving target. We're talking about tolerances in the tens of microns for something like a retinal procedure. So you've got a robot operating at a precision that no human hand can match, and then the patient shifts, or coughs, or startles, or just becomes more alert than expected and tries to look around.

The first thing I'd say is that you cannot treat this as an edge case. When I talk to engineers coming from manufacturing or even from other surgical domains, there's a tendency to think of patient movement as a disturbance you reject, like vibration on a factory floor. That framing is wrong. The patient is not noise. The patient is a participant whose state is changing, and the system has to model that.

So we think about it in layers. The outermost layer is detection: can the system recognize that the patient's state is changing before the movement actually becomes dangerous? That means fusing a lot of signals. You've got the imaging, obviously, the intraoperative OCT or the microscope feed showing you where the eye is. But you also have force sensing at the instrument tip, you have the anesthesiologist's monitors, you might have eye tracking on the contralateral eye. And a lot of what we've learned is that the precursors to a patient becoming agitated show up in those secondary signals before they show up as gross motion.

The second layer is the response itself, and here's where I think the field has sometimes gotten it backwards. The instinct is to say, well, the robot should retract. Get the instrument out, get to safety. But in the eye, a fast retraction can be more dangerous than holding position, because you can tear tissue on the way out. So the "safe" response is actually highly context dependent. If I'm inside the retina with a membrane peeling instrument, the safest thing might be to hold absolutely still and let the surgeon decide. If I'm at the surface, retract. And the robot has to know which situation it's in.

That's where the learning piece comes in, and I'll be candid about the limitations. We can't train this on real patient emergencies at scale, for obvious reasons. So we lean heavily on simulation, on phantom models, on data from procedures where nothing went wrong but where we can observe the natural variability of patient motion. And we try to learn policies that are conservative by default. I'd rather have a system that pauses too often than one that makes a confident wrong move.

The third layer, and this is the one I think gets undervalued, is the human handoff. The surgeon is still in the room. The anesthesiologist is still in the room. When the patient wakes up, the robot's job isn't to solve the problem alone. Its job is to get to a stable state and communicate clearly and fast about what it's doing and why. If the surgeon has to spend three seconds figuring out what the robot just did, that's three seconds we've lost.

So when people ask me about training a robot for this, I usually push back on the framing a little. It's not really about training the robot to respond. It's about designing a system where the robot, the surgeon, and the care team have a shared understanding of what happens when things go sideways, and the learned components are there to buy time and preserve safety margins, not to be the hero.

r001.rationale: The response discusses context-dependent instrument retraction, but does not identify withdrawing an endoscope or say that it contributed to a manageable outcome when a patient woke during eye surgery.

astra-6.text:
I think the first challenge is defining what we mean by “respond.” If a patient wakes up or starts moving during eye surgery, we don’t necessarily want a robot to improvise. We want it to recognize that something has changed, understand the limits of what it knows, and put the surgeon in a position to respond safely.

That’s also a difficult training problem because these are events you hope happen very rarely. You can’t deliberately create dangerous situations just to collect examples. Simulation could help us explore different scenarios, but then we have to ask how well that training carries over to a real patient.

So I’d frame it less as teaching a robot to handle every possible emergency and more as teaching it when to stop, when to signal uncertainty, and when to hand control back to the clinical team.

r001.rationale: The response discusses recognizing changes, simulation, and handing control to the clinical team, but does not mention withdrawing the endoscope or connect it to a manageable outcome.

sol-6.1.text: The challenge is that you’re asking a robot to respond to something unpredictable in a setting where even a small movement can matter. If a patient wakes up or starts to move, the right response may be to stop and let the surgeon take over. So it’s not just about training the robot to perform the procedure; it’s about teaching it to recognize when the situation has changed and when it needs help. How do you give it enough experience with those rare events, and then demonstrate that it responds safely?

r001.rationale: The response says the robot may need to stop and let the surgeon take over, but does not identify withdrawing the endoscope as contributing to a manageable outcome.
